style: tech blog intro paragraph about migrating from MySQL to PostgreSQL (not a job posting)
text: So we finally did it. After three years of "we should really move off MySQL" in every planning meeting, we actually shipped the migration last month, and I'm still not 100% sure whether to be relieved or terrified. Honestly it went better than I expected, mostly because Priya refused to let us skip the dry runs (we did four, and the last one still surfaced a timezone bug in our reporting jobs that would've been ugly in prod). This post is a brief rundown of what we moved, what hurt, and a few things I wish someone had told us before we started. Fair warning: some of this is specific to our setup (roughly 2TB, a couple hundred tables, a Django monolith with way too much raw SQL in it), so your mileage will vary. We're not going to pretend PostgreSQL is objectively better across the board, because it isn't, but for our workload the JSONB support, better handling of concurrent writes, and the query planner finally made our analytics team stop filing tickets about the same three slow joins. Anyway, grab a coffee, here's the messy version.

text:
Title: Backend dev 6 yrs, thinking about moving into ML. Is it worth it or am I late?

Hey all, lurker here mostly, first real post. Throwaway-ish account, don't want coworkers finding this lol.

Quick background: I've been a backend engineer for about 6 years, mostly Python and Go, some Java before that. Currently at a mid-sized fintech doing payments infra. I like the work fine, the team is good, pay is decent. But I've been feeling kind of restless for like a year now and I keep ending up on ML stuff at 1am.

What I've done so far:
- Finished Andrew Ng's ML course (the old Coursera one, not the new one, I think I did it in 2019 and forgot most of it lol)
- Did a couple fast.ai lessons, got through maybe 3 of the 7 or so
- Built a small sentiment classifier on some scraped tweets for a side project, it works ok, accuracy is fine but the whole thing is held together with duct tape
- Been doing a few Kaggle titanic-style competitions, nothing impressive, top 40% on one

I'm not a total beginner with the math honestly? Linear algebra is fine, I did a stats minor in undergrad (calc-based probability was rough tho). Gradient descent makes sense to me. Backprop I understand conceptually but I couldn't derive it cleanly on a whiteboard without looking stuff up.

My questions:
1. Is it realistic to switch to an ML engineer role (not research, I don't have a PhD and don't want one) coming from backend? I keep seeing "MLE" postings that look a lot like backend with some model serving stuff. Maybe that's my in?
2. Should I go back and do a master's? My company would pay for part of it but it's a part-time online program and I'm not sure it's worth the time. Or is a portfolio enough?
3. Is the market for this totally cooked right now? I read a lot of doom posts about layoffs and everyone and their dog doing LLM wrappers. Kinda scared I'm trying to enter at the worst possible time.
4. If you made this switch, what did you wish you'd known? Especially what you'd skip.

Also if anyone has opinions on whether I should just stay in backend and get good at the ML infra side (feature stores, serving, pipelines) instead of trying to be the person training models, I'd love to hear that. Feels like a more honest fit for my actual skills tbh.

Thanks for reading the wall of text. Appreciate any real talk, including "you're overthinking this."

Edit: a few people asked, yes I know I should just pick one and start. Working on it.
